artifacts.notes: Keyed text, not OCR, and that distinction is the whole finding here. guidance/catena.md records that Migne PL 34's Internet Archive text layer corrupts roughly one word in eight and concluded that "the unencumbered Latin is OCR wreckage and the clean Latin is encumbered". That is true of the scan and false of the volume: this is the University of Zurich's Corpus Corporum TEI encoding of the same columns, keyed rather than scanned, republished on Latin Wikisource under a stated CC BY-SA 4.0 markup licence over a public-domain printing. This is a transcription of a web witness of the 1841 printing and not a collation against the printed column, so no passage taken from it rises above inspected.

artifacts.notes: The pages carry the Corpus Corporum encoding note recording that the file was encoded in TEI XML for the University of Zurich's Corpus Corporum project by Ph. Roelli in 2013 from Migne's Patrologia Latina tomus 34. That is the encoder's statement about the file and is not part of Migne; the transformation below removes it. This retrieval also settles, in the opposite direction from the earlier finding, that PL 34 is reachable as keyed text and not only as the Internet Archive's corrupt scan.
artifacts.rights_basis: Augustine's Latin is of the fifth century and Migne's printing is of 1841, so the text beneath these bytes is in the public domain everywhere. The bytes themselves are the wiki source of a Latin Wikisource transcription, and Latin Wikisource contributions are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 — a condition on the contributors' markup rather than on Migne's text under it. The exact bytes are therefore hashed and recorded but not retained here, and only the printed Latin reaches the tracked derivative.

passages.context: The whole of book X of De Genesi ad litteram as Migne prints it in Patrologia Latina 34, in all 25 of the paragraphs the printing gives it, the running head and the Maurist argument included. The argument reads only "In quo tractatur de animarum origine" and names NO verse of Genesis. The extent is therefore declared at Genesis 2:7, the verse whose treatment in books VI and VII this book continues — the inbreathing from which the question of the soul's origin arises — and that anchor is this project's inference from the argument and not a statement Migne makes.

alternate_titles: De Genesi ad litteram libri duodecim
On Genesis according to the letter
Sur la Genese au sens litteral
work.author: Augustine of Hippo
work.description: Augustine's third and longest commentary on the opening of Genesis, written between about 401 and 415 and running to twelve books. It reaches Genesis 3 and no further: books I to III expound the six days, IV to IX the second chapter, and XI the fall, while X on the origin of souls and XII on paradise and the third heaven are excursuses the earlier books provoked. It is 'ad litteram' in Augustine's own sense of asking what happened rather than what it signifies, which he distinguishes in book I from the figurative reading he had given in De Genesi contra Manichaeos. Distinct from the abandoned De Genesi ad litteram imperfectus liber, which is a separate work and a separate record.
work.title: De Genesi ad litteram
